speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising to make a statement about the possibility of concluding this part of the session today. There have been a number of discussions among the representatives of the various parties and I believe that we have a basis for proceeding, which is that we would adjourn, following royal assent to the Olympic bill, until October 15 barring any emergency that would require the recalling of the House.
We have also provided for a method of dealing with the capital punishment bill, Bill C-2. It would be dealt with under certain conditions which are specified in the motion. They are, that on the first day the order is called we would deal with the amendments at the report stage, and then we would have third reading, with extended hours, without any amendments and with the length of speeches being limited, but not their number. Finally, we have agreed that we will have the vote on third reading at a time to be agreed upon by representatives of the parties. On the basis of that statement, I wish to seek unanimous consent to have this motion moved by my colleague, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury).
May I also seek the consent of the House, once this motion is put by unanimous consent, not to proceed with debate on the motion immediately, in order that we may deal with another matter, namely, the Olympic bill. If we could call it immediately, by consent, it would get to the other place and it might be possible for us to adjourn after royal assent at about four o'clock.
May I first ask for consent to have the motion moved by my colleague. If that is forthcoming, I will then ask for consent not to proceed with debate on the motion, and call Government orders solely for the purpose of giving third reading to the Olympic bill.

Mr. Speaker, I do not quite understand what the minister has in mind with respect to the capital punishment bill. Does this mean it is off until October? If that is so, will he advise the House what the attitude of the government will be respecting applications that may come before the government between now and
October, on behalf of convicted persons, for commutation of the death sentence?

speechtext:
I should like to point out, also, that on the same day the hon. member for High Park-Humber Valley stated that to win a gold medal was the goal of every athlete, and that the Olympics offered such an opportunity. It seems to me that is opposite to the view expressed yesterday when the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling) read the Olympic creed which states that the most important thing in the Olympic games is not to win, but to take part. I suggest this is just the same as life; the most important thing is not to triumph, but to struggle. When we consider the forerunner to the Olympic games, we think of the Pythian games which were held in Greek times; we find that the first prize was a cauldron and the second prize was an unblemished fair maiden. As history would have it, everyone strove to be second, not first.
This leads me to ask whether this is what we are striving for. Is that what we are training people to accomplish, as far as the Olympic games are concerned? Is the purpose to win a gold medal? Is that the purpose for which we embark on any kind of sport program in this country- to be first? Is that the important point? I think that is what is wrong with the whole concept of the Olympic games, apart from the financial aspects of this bill. It seems to me that to be first is not the important thing but, rather, the important thing is preparing the athletes involved, preparing young people through an athletics program that is ongoing, rather than for three or four years in order that they can make an Olympics team and win a gold medal.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, two days ago an hon. gentleman, speaking on the bill, stated there was opposition to the financing proposals for these games. He said there was confusion. I suggest that if there is confusion about the financing of these games, that hon. member should not stand in this House and vote for the bill, particularly when members of his party raise legitimate questions about the way in which the games are being financed. Speaking on behalf of the Conservative Party, the hon. member said they will not accept any further financial obligation. That sounds to me as hollow as bamboo. As a matter of fact, hon. members to my right seem to be taking the position of what I call a mugwump. If you do not know what a mugwump is, let me explain.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are some brief comments I think I ought to make before the question is put on the adjournment motion. First of all, with regard to the statement made by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEac-hen) when he referred to the adjournment being to October 15, it is possible to interpret his remarks to indicate that the date October 15 was part of an all-party agreement. I should like to make clear that we in this party have not agreed to the date October 15. The selection of that date and the adjournment until that date is clearly the responsibility of the government. I wish to make very clear that we have not agreed to an adjournment of that length of time.
At this time I do not intend to review the work of the session and what has or has not been done, but I do wish to make a brief reference to two great problems which confront the country, as it is now being proposed that this House adjourn. The first problem to which I should like to refer briefly is, of course, the dispute between the railway companies and the non-operating unions-a matter of great concern-a dispute which is capable of doing great damage to the economy of the country as well as cause great inconvenience to the Canadian people.
We have been pressing the minister for some time to accept his responsibility, intervene in this dispute and play an active role in trying to bring the parties together with a view to settling the dispute and avoiding possible disruption of the Canadian economy. The minister's atti-

July 27, 1973
Summer Recess
tude has been that he believes in the collective bargaining process and that it should continue. He has expressed belief in the good sense of the parties to the dispute. He says that if it seems to be desirable or in the public interest, he will play any role which seems to him to be proper, and if it becomes necessary the government will do what it ought to do. It seems to me and to the members of my party that the minister has been displaying a very casual attitude. The situation appears to be degenerating. We now have selective strikes taking place. We have the danger, at least, of retaliation from the railway companies. There is the possibility of lockouts, either partial or complete. The country is therefore faced, as this adjournment motion is before the House, with the possibility of grave disruption in the essential elements of our transportation system.
It is in this atmosphere that the government is proposing the adjournment of the House. I want to make it very clear that this is on its own responsibility, and that we are ready to stay here, if necessary, to face up to our responsibility as parliamentarians in this situation which virtually amounts to a crisis. We have been pressing, we continue to press and we shall press today for some assurance from the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) that he is prepared to accept his responsibility as Minister of Labour and intervene actively with a view to bringing the parties back to negotiations and to a settlement. We have had no success in persuading the minister to accept his responsibilities.
The minister and the government are proposing nothing except a "wait and see" attitude, with offers of mediation. Parliament is subject to recall and, of course, we are ready to come back any time, at very short notice, to meet any emergency that may develop. But I say to the minister and to the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Sharp) that the government must not let the economy of this country and the people of this country suffer. There comes a time when the public interest must prevail, and we will expect this government to discharge its responsibility.
Hear, hear!

What we want specifically at this time is some assurance from the minister that he will fully discharge his responsibilities, play an active part and involve himself personally by taking the political risk that is associated with making a personal effort to get this dispute settled.
Hear, hear!
The second great problem that exists and to which I want to refer-
Politics.

Politics? The second problem to which I want to refer, that exists at the time the House is being asked to adjourn, is the rapid increase in the cost of living that is taking place. I say, Sir, that the government has no approach to combat the increasing cost of living except to allow interest rates to increase and the possibility of tight money to develop. I remind the government again that the unemployment figures issued last month were a warning

light that other problems may develop in the economy as a result of a slowdown in the rate of growth of the economy.
We have put forward a specific proposal regarding the fighting of inflation. The government does not accept that-that is its right-but I say that the government has prepared no effective attack on the cost of living, and in this respect the government is not governing.
Hear, hear!
They have not for a long time.

The kind of toothless review board which was set up by the government to review the price of food is no effective response. This government has insisted on holding on to office, and I say that if it is going to hold on to office it will have to discharge its responsibilities to the Canadian people. If anybody on that side of the House thinks the government will get away from opposition pressure on these issues just by having the House adjourn, I suspect he is in for a surprise. I know that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) expressed the view three or four years ago that all of us in the opposition were nobodies once we were a few hundred feet from Parliament Hill.
All members.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Look at what he did when he was away.

I just want to say that if the Minister of Labour does not accept his responsibilities in this railway dispute, and if the government allows the cost of living to continue to escalate as it has been escalating, they will quickly find out who really are the nobodies and how quickly they will become nobodies.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, it is always easy when a motion of this sort is put before the House to sound as if it were somebody else's responsibility and to attack the government for introducing the motion. However, I think in all fairness the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) should have said, as I intended to say, that the motion which is now before the House was agreed to by the leader of the Opposition's party as well as by the other opposition parties in the House.
Oh, oh!
Another Liberal apologist.

I do not think we serve the cause of parliament and the cause of relations among the parties in the House by trying to give the impression, when there has been an all-party agreement, that only one party is responsible for it.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: It took you a week to find that out.

Mr. Speaker, let me remind the members of the Conservative Party-I will come back to that remark in a moment-that before their leader spoke today they went around the House and in the lobbies telling everybody that we would be out of here if it were not for Stanley. These holier than thou people who wanted parlia-
July 27, 1973

ment to recess several days ago are now accusing others of putting the motion at this time. There really should be an end to hypocrisy at some point.
Hear, hear!

Then we have the statement that there is a crisis on the railways-there certainly is-and the Leader of the Opposition and other members of the Conservative Party keep telling the government to do something about it. Let them be honest enough to say that they want the government to bring in a law today ordering the striking railway workers back to work.
Oh, oh!
That is not so.
That is erroneous; it is not correct.
Cheap.
If they are right, and that is not so, that is not what they want-and I hope they are-what, in heaven's name, do they want?
We want the government to live up to its responsibilities.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: May we have order, please. It is extremely difficult for members at this end of the chamber to hear the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis). I would hope that the hon. member who has been recognized will be given an opportunity to make his remarks. Perhaps other hon. members who feel they have comments to make will have the opportunity to speak on the motion later.

Mr. Speaker, I want the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) to live up to his responsibility and I want to make some specific suggestions to him. The idea that if the Minister of Labour appears at the negotiating table tomorrow it will settle the strike is a naive and inexperienced idea. The time for him to appear is when there is an opportunity to settle the strike, which I suspect is not yet here, so demands that the minister go to Montreal and sit down at the negotiating table can only be made by people who know very little about negotiation.
Hear, hear!
But there are things that the Minister of Labour can do now.
Resign.

I invite him to do them. One of the major problems which is embittering the railway employees at the present time is the widespread opposition among them to the pension plans that have been agreed to and the way in which those pension plans are handled by the railways. One of the things that undoubtedly would very quickly ease the situation among the railway employees out on strike would be the Minister of Labour immediately
Summer Recess
appointing an independent inquiry into the railway pension plans.
The minister should appoint someone to make an independent analysis of the railway pension plans, to make an analysis of their actual cost, to make an analysis of the plans in comparison with other industrial plans and with government pension plans. He should divulge to the workers of the railways the facts of their pension plans. If such an inquiry shows they are behind other industrial plans, as they are, and behind government pension plans, as they are, then the inquiry ought to make specific recommendations for changing those plans. Since Canadian National Railways are government-owned, there is no reason in the world why the government and this parliament should not order the CNR to treat their employees as they ought to be treated in the area of pensions.
There is another thing which the minister can do immediately, and in my opinion ought to do, to carry out his responsibility in this matter. It is obvious to anybody who is watching the situation that the railway employees are anxious to exercise their right to strike, and to exercise it in such a way as to minimize the harm it does to the economy and the people of Canada. It is equally obvious that the railways are determined not to let them carry on a strike which will minimize the harm to the economy. It is obvious that the CNR and the CPR in particular are threatening lay-offs, threatening not to recall those who are out on temporary strike, and are deliberately taking action to provoke a general strike or a general lockout in this country, hoping that this parliament will help the railways out by passing the kind of law ordering the employees back to work that some members of this House would like to see passed.
I believe that the Minister of Labour, speaking on behalf of the people of Canada as well as on behalf of the employees of the railways, ought to tell the railways, particularly the CPR and the CNR-more particularly the CNR-to cut out their shenanigans and act like responsible corporations, as they are a public utility of this country.
The railways ought to be requested, and if necessary in some way ordered, to play ball with the unions and to allow the unions to carry on the strike with the least possible damage to the economy of Canada, with the least possible damage to grain shipments and to the ferries that the unions have agreed to run. I say, Mr. Speaker, if the arrangement to work the Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland ferries should break down, and if continuing to ship grain should break down, it will not be the responsibility of the railway workers; it will be the responsibility of the railways and their deliberate provoking of a general strike. That is what will bring about a breakdown of the intentions of the railway unions.
Baloney!

I expected the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), I think it was, or somebody from that group to say "baloney," but I say this is the key to keep the strike under control, doing as little damage as possible to the Canadian economy. The railway workers are suffering from the fact that they are in an essential service. They are given the right, under the law, to take action like

all other workers in this country, outside of certain excepted groups, are permitted to do. But the moment they do that and the moment their strike becomes effective, then everybody screams that they must go back to work because they are in an essential service. I say that men and women who are employed in an essential service in Canada are entitled to the same rights, the same conditions of work and the same decent wages as are all other employees in this country.
Hear, hear!

These are the things that the Minister of Labour can do. I cannot, from my not inconsiderable experience in labour negotiations, tell him that he should go to Montreal tomorrow to the negotiating table because it does not look as though the settlement is there yet. I think that kind of intervention is better at a later stage.
There is a third thing that the minister can do immediately, and no one can stop him, and that is appoint an independent mediator. There is not much value in one of the officials of his department meeting with the unions and the railways. I do not say this because they are not competent, because Mr. Kelly is not a competent negotiator and mediator with a great deal of experience in labour matters, particularly railway labour. However, the Minister of Labour knows as well as I do that at this stage an officer of his department is not going to carry very much weight. He ought to appoint immediately, just as the strike has settled down-with a time limit, not of months but of a week or ten days-an independent mediator of standing in the community. The minister knows such people better than I do. He should appoint someone to go to Montreal, sit down with the two parties and try to squeeze a settlement out of them. In my view, a competent mediator could accomplish that within a relatively short time, a matter of a week or ten days. Particularly would that be the case if the minister appointed an independent inquiry into the pension plans and the monetary value of those pension plans which would give the mediator a chance to obtain the facts on these matters as he discussed them with the parties to the dispute.
These are practical things an independent inquiry into the pension plans, a strong statement by the government to the companies to stop their shenanigans and to co-operate with the unions in having the strike produce as little harm as possible, and the appointment of an independent mediator, a person with experience in the realm of labour relations, who has standing in the community and carries weight with both sides in the dispute. If the minister would do those three concrete things immediately, I think it would do a great deal to shorten the dispute and reduce the danger of real damage, particularly to the farmers of western Canada in the shipment of grain.
Mr. Speaker, on this kind of motion one should not make a lengthy speech. There are various things that concern us, but I do not know that parliament's sitting for another two or three weeks would solve those matters. Of course, it would not. But there are problems that concern us about the cost of living and the general economy. We dealt with them at our convention last week.
I merely want to say to the government House leader, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) that

now that we have a sensible arrangement for completing the debate on Bill C-2, it will take a reasonable time, rather than an unreasonable time, even if there is no time limit. Obviously, it will take a reasonable time to complete that bill. There are on the order paper other bills which we are anxious to debate as quickly as possible. We should deal with the family allowances bill, the election expenses bill, the foreign investments bill-which has been dealt with by the committee and with other bills of that sort.
Finally, I suggest to the leader of the House that while the Senate is sitting and considering the Olympic bill, the crop insurance bill should be brought in and passed this afternoon. We do not see any reason for anyone to object to increased facilities for farmers in the area of crop insurance. That bill ought to pass without debate. If it does not pass, provincial governments will need to carry a much greater load of expense, because they have already reduced premiums in anticipation of the passage of the federal crop insurance bill. I do not see why that should not be done today in a few minutes before we recess.
My colleagues and I are disappointed that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) who is in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board did not find it necessary to come back to this House today, as it was his duty to do. Some time ago he gave an undertaking to the House in reply to a question by my colleague, the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Gleave)-who is also not here; I must say that in fairness. The minister undertook to make a statement on the government's new policy on feed grains before this House rose for the summer.
It was his duty as a minister, and his moral duty-in view of his undertaking-to be present and to make that statement. His failure to be here is an affront to the House. What is more important, it leaves the farmers of this country in uncertainty. It leaves them in the position of not knowing what is happening, and it leaves the government in an unhappy position. If it is stupid enough to take the authority for feed grains away from the Canadian Wheat Board, it will suffer even worse consequences on the prairies next when there is an election than it did the last time.
I end on the note on which I started. We agree to the motion, but not to the date of October 15 for the recalling of parliament. We would have preferred parliament to be recalled one or two weeks earlier. However, that is not a matter of such import now, in view of the present situation. We agree to the motion because we think it necessary, particularly in view of the railway strike, for the minister to have a chance to work at it, for the government to bear its responsibilities and take action, and for parliament to be recalled if that action is not satisfactory. We feel that parliament has done useful work in the present session. We expect the fall sitting to be productive of even more useful things. That we shall see when we come back, Sir.

Mr. Speaker, if the sessions opened and adjourned on set dates, as is done in Great Britain, in France and in many other countries, we would not witness the show we had this morning.
July 27, 1973

The hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis), Leader of the New Democratic Party, is entirely right when he says that under an agreement made among the various parties we will be adjourning till October 15.
However, the Leader of the Progressive Conservative Party (Mr. Stanfield) rises offended and blames the government for introducing the motion to adjourn. He says that he is prepared to carry on and remain here. Mr. Speaker, for at least three weeks, I have been meeting Progressive Conservative members telling me: "When will the session end? When will we be on holidays?" Some have already left. Indeed, we noted it last evening. Thirty members present out of 107, that is not too bad.
Mr. Speaker, we all agree that during this session we would have liked to discuss the economic surge. We would have liked to discuss right away about family allowances so as to start paying them on September 1 instead of January 1. The consumers' purchasing power should be tailored to the cost of living through compensated discounts. We would have liked to speak about conflicts which exist throughout Canada.
The member for York South mentioned the railway dispute and said that it was no time for the Minister of Labour (M. Munro) to intervene. I maintain that he should have intervened much sooner, that is to say he should have been preventive instead of curative so as to prevent disastrous strikes from occurring. Everyone wants the railway workers to be well treated but we have had railway strikes before. It has been said that the problem was settled and today again we have a new railway strike. Therefore, I am right when I say that a strike does not settle the labour problem. A strike is no help to a worker because it is at his own expenses. The only ones benefiting from a strike are the labour leaders, the strike organizers and the union lawyers. This is why I have been asking them for 30 years: Show me a strike which helped settled the labour issue in Canada or elswhere in the world. Strikes in the USSR led to a regime set up 60 years ago. Did that settle the problem?
There are no strikes in the USSR!

They no longer have strikes precisely because guys like the New Democrats hold power in the USSR. Through their work and in the name of freedom, union leaders succeeded in overthrowing the regime which existed then. And today former union leaders are at the head of USSR departments and people are forbidden from striking. If a worker is planning a strike he is immediately shot or deported to Siberia. That is what those people would like to give Canada!
Ha! Ha! Real!
There they are: they say "Ha!" We need only read the Regina manifesto; it says the same thing that occurred in Russia, in Czechoslovakia.
Give it to us!

For sure! Mr. Speaker, you hear them. Questions have been asked about the rail dispute for two weeks now. It has not been solved and the minister is told: You must act. It is obvious that if the
Summer Recess
minister introduces a bill in the House, it will be to order the workers back to work. To my mind, it would be much more logical to guarantee them security and freedom, through a government measure, than to allow them to be pushed around by the socialists and communists who head the unions in the province of Quebec.
Come on, Real, that is not true; that is an insult.

You won't tell me that Laberge is not a socialist right through and through. He said so himself.
Mr. Speaker, I understand. People say lawyers live off the unions. The hon. member for York South knew it before he became a member. Those are the people who accuse me of being against the unions. I am in favour of them provided they are controlled by the members and not by people like Laberge, Pepin, Chartrand, and perhaps soon, in some cases, by the hon. member for York South.
But there are good unions. They exist.

There are unions. Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) was a union man too. He has improved. I believe that he received the sanctifying grace of the liberal party!
Mr. Speaker, my riding is a working-class riding, the people work in the farming and forestry industries, and there are thousands of miners who belong to unions. I have often been invited to come and help settle disputes. Though I was not a negotiator myself I met with the negotiators and said to them: Do your job yourselves, I will not interfere. I also met with the employers and with the workers and their wives and sometimes even the children.
When the women didn't have any milk, they would say: Jean-Baptiste, go out and work. But Jean-Baptiste was on strike and it lasted for quite some time. I was obliged to intervene in many disputes, at Val-d'Or, at Malartic, at Rouyn-Noranda, and I was never afraid to tell the workers' leaders what I thought, to their faces, not behind their backs. I also said to the workers, and I say it again, here in the House this time: Go ahead and join the unions, but take control of them yourselves. Don't let yourselves be controlled by trouble-makers like the ones we find everywhere in Canada nowadays. I know a fellow in Montreal who has just left the Canadian Labour Congress because his life was threatened by members of the CLC in Montreal. Mr. Speaker, what was solved by the strikes in the construction industry? Two years ago there was a general strike of construction workers throughout Quebec. In Rouyn the people wanted to build a composite school, but what happened? Three vehicles arrived from Montreal carrying 16 union thugs who threatened the people, saying that they would beat them up, break their legs and set fire to their houses.
Mr. Speaker, you are about to rise, and I am about to take my seat. In any event, the four parties in this House have agreed that we adjourn until October 15. I hope that the railway employees dispute will be settled as quickly as possible, and I hope that when the House reconvenes, we will get on with the business of passing legislation that
26454-18J

July 27, 1973
Summer Recess
will give the people of Canada security, and freedom, and not slavery.
[ English]

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of Labour):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have listened to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), the leader of the New Democratic Party and the leader of the Social Credit Party. May I first make reference to the comments of the Leader of the Opposition. As Minister of Labour, I do not need the pious pontifica-tion of the Leader of the Opposition to remind me what my responsibilities are to the Canadian people; nor do we need the pious pontification of the Leader of the Opposition to remind this government of its responsibilities.
Hear, hear!

We are fully aware of the serious implications of a railway strike in this country. Who wouldn't be? For us to act now would be an arbitrary denial, before a complete strike takes place, of the workers' rights to express their dissatisfaction with their working conditions and rates of pay.
The party which the Leader of the Opposition leads, the Progressive Conservative Party, is well on record as endorsing the principle of free collective bargaining in the long term public interest. I assume that is their justification for endorsing that philosophy. Be it so-called essential services or not, it can be argued, and I think has been argued successfully within the councils of the Progressive Conservative party, that free collective bargaining, in the long run, is in the public interest.
The Leader of the Opposition says he wants my assurance that I will accept my responsibility. He has that assurance, as do the people of Canada. I think there was some cynicism exhibited in the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition. He said I should personally intervene. If he means by that personal intervention, this also carries with it the connotation that the government should come forward with a bill that would intervene-
No.
It is sophistry.

It is not sophistry. The Leader of the Opposition shakes his head in a negative way. I take it the official position of this party is that he is not recommending at this stage legislation that would impose a settlement or force the men back to work. What alternatives is he suggesting? He has suggested personal intervention on my part. I have personally intervened whenever I found that intervention would be constructive.
In this particular case, I quite agree with the leader of the New Democratic Party when he says that personal intervention by a Minister of Labour does not necessarily lead to a settlement, and in some cases is not even conducive to reaching a settlement. It is misleading to the Canadian people to suggest that intervention by a Minister of Labour by somehow corralling the parties, taking them by the scruff of the neck, throwing them in a room and walking out will lead to a settlement. It just does not

work that way. I know the Leader of the Opposition is fully aware of that.
The Leader of the Opposition said we should take the political risks. That is not even a factor of my thinking or the thinking of the government. Trying to arrive at a settlement of this particular dispute is the overriding concern; politics is not a consideration at all.
Hear, hear!

While talking about politics, I might say that to try and resolve this dispute with minimal dislocation to the country, Canadians and the employees involved is a two-way street. Alarm that is injected purposely, and to some degree falsely, is not conducive to trying to arrive at a settlement of this dispute.
To play on people's fears by exaggerating the implications, however serious they may be, indicating that the country is somehow going to be on the verge of economic disaster if something does not occur right away, is to mislead the Canadian people. That type of responsibility should be exhibited by members of the opposition as well as by members of the government.
Will the minister permit a question?

If the right hon. member does not mind, I have just about finished my remarks. With regard to the comments of the leader of the Social Credit party, accusations of a most exaggerated kind as to political affiliation, and derogatory terms about leaders of the labour movement, are also not conducive to arriving at a settlement of this dispute and the serious implications of it.
I have noted the comments made by the leader of the New Democratic Party. He mentioned three things. He spoke of pensions. He said there ought to be an independent adjudicator, a man with high qualifications and experience in the field, who would examine the situation and make recommendations. I have already said that this suggestion is being given serious consideration at the present moment.
As to appeals to the employers-the hon. gentleman put it more strongly than that-not to take any action which would exacerbate an already serious situation, such appeals have been made and I hope they carry some weight.
As to the services of a competent mediator being provided at some stage in the dispute, consideration is being given to this proposal. The proposition is arguable, I believe, in the present circumstances, but the idea is certainly being given consideration.
I want to assure members of the House and the Canadian people that we do not belittle the implications of this impending strike, particularly in view of the dislocation caused by the commencement of rotating strikes. We shall do everything possible within our ability to bring this dispute to an end.
July 27, 1973
Would the minister now be prepared to accept a question?
Yes.

It is simply this. The minister has stated he is doing everything he can, and that the situation is serious. If the situation we have seen in the last few days continues, how long will it be before the government considers taking effective action?

Mr. Speaker, that is a hypothetical question. The right hon. member very well knows we have to consider the implications, and weigh the inconvenience to the public against the philosophy and principles of free collective bargaining, which are also very real and which are also in the public interest. The point at which these two considerations come into balance is a matter of judgment to be reached in the circumstances.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to say much in response to the statement made by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro). In so far as he has a case-and I doubt whether he has much of a case-it will be dealt with by other members of my party. I will say only this: he based his case, such as it is, on the extent to which he has a responsibility to exercise. It is the opinion of members of this party that this responsibility has not been exercised, that the minister's position is that of Mr. Micawber in David Copperfield; he sits back, hoping that something will happen.
Nonsense.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
We believe there is a case to be made for the government and the minister exercising ingenuity and diligence and working hard in an effort to develop, through their own initiatives, a solution lying between the necessity of having to take parliamentary action and their sitting on their seats doing nothing. We think there is an intermediate ground but that the government and the minister have not been diligent enough to find it. That is our complaint.
With regard to the remarks of the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis), I was prepared to take issue with him, but in the latter part of his speech he did put into context the position of the various House leaders with regard to the motion before us. We worked to produce an order with particular reference to the amendments to the Criminal Code. That is common knowledge. Even the Chair might take judicial notice of the fact that this was the "sticker" with which we were confronted. I pay tribute to my colleagues in the other parties for their work in reaching a compromise which was acceptable to members in all quarters.
In working out this order our minds were directed to the details required to develop a solution which would find some measure of general acceptance. There was no suggestion of dealing with any matter beyond this. The government House leader, as was his duty, indicated the intention of the government with regard to an adjournment date. This was within our knowledge and I wish to make it plain that it is not our intention to oppose this motion in
Summer Recess
its present terms. On that issue, bearing in mind the grave problems which confront the country, the responsibility is one which falls squarely on the shoulders of the government. It is for the government to take that responsibility and to answer for it if and when the occasion arises.
When an hon. member comes to consider his position with regard to an adjournment motion, I think he asks himself: What are the serious problems which confront the country and what hope exists that legislative or other proposals will be forthcoming from the government which would amount at least to a reasonable attempt to find solutions? My immediate impulse would be to say the House should not be allowed to depart and the Parliament should not be allowed to adjourn as long as these problems continue to exist and there is hope that legislative proposals can be advanced to deal with them. But in this light, we are surely entitled to examine the government's record-its rather pitiful attempts to deal with other problems. We are entitled to compare what was promised in the Speech from the Throne with what has been brought forward, and to ask ourselves whether there is any reason we should object to this motion, and say to Parliament: Stay here.
In the light of its record, in the light of what the government has done and failed to do, I must say to myself, as I am sure a good many members of the other side of the House say to themselves-because they dare not say it aloud: Why in the name of Heaven keep Parliament in session, having regard to the pitiful record of the government in bringing forward legislation to deal with the problems of the country?
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: If it would be of any value, I could place the legislative record before the House. Apart from appropriation measures, 13 bills have received Royal Assent.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Twenty-seven.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The hon. member and I part company on that. I am not talking about measures which were passed. I am talking about measures which received Royal Assent. Maybe His Excellency has been here at a time of which I did not receive notice. Consider that list with the measures listed in the Speech from the Throne, those glorious, golden promises contained in the Speech from the Throne.
We all remember sitting here and listening to the government tell us, in the words of His Excellency, that it would continue its discussions with the United States to settle certain difficulties which had arisen in our trading arrangements with that country, and to promote stable economic growth. And today, six months later, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) is starting to fight. Six months have been spent in making an appreciation of the situation and acquiring the intelligence needed.
I would ask those hon. members who are doing their jobs as representatives of the housewives and the people of this country who buy foodstuffs and clothing and the housing they need to contrast the situation which exists

July 27, 1973
Summer Recess
today with this promise to promote stable economic growth and attain reasonable price stability.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I note that the applause of the Secretary of State for External Affairs is as weak as his fight. The next promise was a major revision of the general adjustment assistance plan to enable industry to take advantage of opportunities for increasing our foreign trade, followed by aid to small businesses through new incentives to strengthen management.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Again we hear some weak applause.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is a weak speech, that is the problem.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
We then find reference to extension and improvement of the Industrial Development Bank. We have had an announcement but we will probably wait months for legislation. There is reference to assistance to co-operative and credit unions, and that bill is on the order paper. Then there is reference to renewed measures to reduce deeply entrenched regional economic disparities, and a review of research and development incentive programs. There is also reference to a social security system containing incentives to work, with greater emphasis on the need to get people on social aid back to work.
I could take hours and hours showing how these golden promises made by the government, which now read like the Arabian Nights fables, contrast to the actual pitiful, atrocious legislative record in respect of which we have to go back and apologize to our constituents. On that basis, with this government's record of ineptness in respect of its administrative accomplishments, what would be the use of trying to stay here to deal with these problems at this time, much as we would like to?
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I am not one of those who say that because this is a minority government it cannot act, because it is not a minority government. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) are equally guilty of parroting the phrase "Our main objective has been to make minority parliament work". There are two things wrong with that phrase: This is not a minority Parliament and it does not work.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The hon. member for York South led his 31 paper tigers back from Vancouver not so long ago.
Covered with bedsores.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
He made some challenging statements about what he was going to do to the government, knowing well that we were coming close to adjournment, and knowing well that the only occasion on which they dared show their teeth was when we in this party had already indicated in respect of certain measures that we intended to support them. Only on those occasions did the junior

partner of this coalition government indicate his willingness to fight. What a party and what a fight, Mr. Speaker.
I want to conclude by referring to two other issues. What concerns me and must concern us all, without regard to partisanship or region, and without regard to any other issue at all, is what is going to happen to the people of this country and our economic situation during the time when we will be absent, until October 15?
When we examine the situation that is developing in the United States, when we realize the extent to which they are rationing certain items, when we read about housewives in that country buying foodstuffs and hoarding, and when we read that people are now anticipating that before the year is over there will be a considerable food shortage, we must realize that it is inevitable that the same situation will develop here to some degree. I want to ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) and the members of the cabinet who are here: If this situation does develop, what do they intend to do about it? Do they intend to call Parliament back? Ministers talked about a contingency plan. Does the government have a contingency plan which can be introduced without legislative authority? Is there any way by which this government can act in the event of that type of emergency arising?
I do not want to hear a lot of nonsense such as that which we heard from the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro)-that the government has a responsibility. It has responsibility for creating the situation, but we on this side of the House have a responsibility for calling to the attention of the government something it seems to have forgotten in its rather selfish attitude about staying in power without regard for the real problems of the country that are developing.
It is almost inevitable that this situation will develop into crisis proportions on the North American continent. Therefore, we are entitled to be told before we leave this place what the government proposes to do. Obviously the government is not able to tell us in chapter and verse precisely what it plans, but will it need parliamentary approval or does it have authority without calling parliament back to deal with the situation? Is it, as I suspect, waiting with faith and hope that something will turn up? This is what we are entitled to know before leaving this place, and I urge the government to give a categorical assurance to members of this House that there are in existence and under consideration plans to deal with this emergency.
If the government does not give us some idea what those plans are, this will be, in our view and in the view of the people of Canada, a further reason why we should have no confidence in this government or in the Liberal party of which it is composed.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, there is one more reason I should have liked this House to continue sitting. I have been for some time trying to obtain an agreement from the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) to institute a commission of inquiry into what appears to be a potentially very serious situation involving fraud and corruption in connection with certain student co-operative building projects in which the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has been involved. The minister has told us that
July 27, 1973

he instituted an in-house or internal inquiry last February.
The facts in connection with this sordid situation, as they appear from sworn evidence, have been publicly known since November, 1971. The statements of a senior adviser to CMHC are on record and give in some detail the facts of this very serious situation involving the CMHC and the government. We do not accept the fact that the minister has launched any meaningful inquiry. If this Parliament recesses today without the government doing something about this, I would take that as being prima facie proof of the fact it is aware of the existence of these facts but is afraid to do anything about the matter.
I conclude in respect of this issue by simply putting on record extracts from the sworn testimony of Mr. Vincent Lapetina, given in the Supreme Court of Ontario on November 3, 1971. He talks about contractors, architects and other people. This testimony was sworn before a Commissioner for Oaths on his examination in respect of an affidavit. He refers to "Murphy" who was one of the contractors, and states:
-Murphy was negotiating the contract for the Waterloo project, there was a certain deal worked out between Murphy and the architects, Tampold Wells, and Howard Edelmann. The deal was that C.M.H.C. requires open bids on jobs; the deal was that Murphy was to get the job regardless of the open bids, but the profits were to be split three ways between Tampold Wells, Howard Edelmann and Murphy. This was done, and the tenders were rigged. I delivered the Murphy bid after the actual bids were opened, delivered it personally to John Wells.
Then there is one more sentence later on:
Bids would be called; Murphy was to get the job; profits were to be split three ways between Murphy, Tampold Wells and Howard Edelmann. Okay? And this was done on the various projects. At this time they had to look for a vehicle to get the funds from Murphy Construction, or Galway Realty into something where Tampold Wells could share on the profits. This is when Winal Properties was incorporated.
I suggest that if the minister is not aware of the facts he should be. There is a responsibility upon him and this government to launch not the kind of inquiry that could only be collateral to a cover-up but a full, unabridged inquiry through a royal commission, so that the people of Canada can know something about these facts. The failure of the government to do something about this before Parliament leaves here today, I suggest, is strong evidence that at least some members of the government know about this, but are afraid and do not want to act.

speakeroldname: Mr. Norman A. Cafik (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion placed before us today by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) contains two basic elements; one that the House be adjourned today until October 15, and the other an agreement on how the bill on capital punishment will be dealt with after that adjournment. I have no quarrel or objection in respect of the agreement concerning this important bill after the House reconvenes on October 15. However, I must admit I have some severe reservations in respect of the date set today for adjournment, October 15.
Summer Recess
I should like to outline, if I may, the reason for my concern; it is very specifically related to a problem of very great significance to the people I happen to represent. I am speaking about the airport at Pickering. The people in Pickering and the immediate area of Markham were concerned by an announcement on March 22, 1971 to the effect that the government proposed to build an airport in the Pickering area.
It is now two and a half years later and this question, even in theory, has not been resolved. The severe uncertainty affecting the lives of hundreds and indeed thousands of people today in that area is still present. I believe it is essential that we eliminate this degree of uncertainty one way or another and as soon as possible.
In addition to the very severe uncertainty there is the question of the credibility not only of the government but more specifically of the Department of Transport. The Department of Transport made this announcement, and has made subsequent announcements since that time which I think leave much to be desired. As I pointed out earlier, the announcement was made on March 22, 1971, two and a half years ago. On August 31, 1972 a further agreement was finally publicly made in the House of Commons. On the dates of August 31 and September 1, 1972, as recorded in Hansard at pages 3897 and 3940, in response to questions raised by myself it was stated that the government would in fact have an independent inquiry, a broad inquiry, allowing input by people in the area, others in the metropolitan area, the provincial government and municipal governments.
That was quite some time ago. What has happened since that time? After the magnificent delay of many months, almost a year, on June 21, 1973 the terms of reference for such an inquiry were announced. In my view, those terms of reference live up to the commitment made nearly a year before. The agreement was that there would be an inquiry conducted by an independent group and that group would be allowed to make recommendations to the government of Canada.
Ever since then there have been many delays. The three independent people have not been named to that inquiry board. Shortly after that announcement of June 21 I raised a question in the House of Commons asking when that inquiry group would be named. The minister gave, if I recall it correct, a rather vague answer and I put the question in more specific terms. The minister then said it would be reasonable to assume that the composition of that board would be announced within a two-week period. To date that board has not yet been named.
I view an adjournment at this time with grave reservations, because at least when the House is in session and I am here and the ministers and others are here I can feel some confidence that I can exert daily pressure upon these people to see that something is in fact done, and done soon. I have reservations because there is the other side to the coin. When the House is adjourned and ministers have more available time, by not having to be in the House on a daily basis, they could direct more of their attention to the problem. In spite of this I have a deep and abiding fear that it is possible that we will wait until after the House comes back for the announcement concerning the naming of people to that independent board.

July 27, 1973
Summer Recess
This would be unacceptable to the people who have waited this great length of time. They deserve better, and they will get better if I have anything to do with it. We need a commitment from this government before this House adjourns today that it will in fact treat this matter with the kind of priority it deserves, and that the people of my area will be relieved of the agonizing uncertainty to which they have been subjected because of the lack of action on the part of the government over such a long, extended period of time.
I am willing not to oppose an adjournment if in fact I can be assured that action will be taken during this adjournment period to speed up the process and name those people within the next week or so, rather than use the adjournment as a medium to extend the delay and thus further the agonizing process to which the people concerned have been subjected.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words about the motion before the House. It provides for a recess and also makes special arrangements to deal with Bill C-2, the capital punishment legislation, when we come back in the fall. I must say that I have seldom been involved in negotiations that were so tough and so determined so far as the parties on both sides were concerned, and yet out of these negotiations we did reach a settlement which, I suppose, is typical in that both sides gave a bit and both sides feel they won.
The fact of the matter is that all of this week there has been terrific pressure from members of all of the other parties in this House for us to get out this week, indeed today, but the issue at stake was, of course, Bill C-2. Those who take the retentionist position were very determined not to agree to any order that would cut off debate. In other words, they would not consent to any time limit on the debate. Yet, I think it can be said that it was for the most part those on the retentionist side who were most anxious to get out.
Those of us who are abolitionists felt very strongly that we did not want the fall session to be jeopardized by a lengthy debate on Bill C-2, and therefore we were equally strong in our position that we were not going to agree to an adjournment of that debate until the fall unless there was an agreement to limit the debate at that time. These positions seemed irreconcilable. Perhaps what we have achieved might be an example to the companies and the unions, in the railway dispute, namely, that irreconcilable positions can be reconciled at some point. What we have achieved is an arrangement which does not provide for a cut-off of the debate in the fall at a precise time, but it does provide for extra hours, shorter speeches and no amendments. The practical effect is that the debate in the fall can hardly last more than five or six days.
It is one of those collective agreements in which both sides have won. The side that did not want a time limit has before the House an order in which there is no time limit. Those of us who wanted the debate to have a practical time limit have won in the sense that there cannot be more than five or six days of debate on capital punishment when we come back to this bill in the fall.
Another issue among us was whether it was desirable to settle the issue now or have it settled in the fall. Those who share my view on the issue-the abolitionist point of view-felt that the issue has been debated long enough, that it was desirable not to have it re-opened in the fall but that it was desirable to get it settled now before we leave. We have conceded that the decision is to be made in the fall. We may be somewhat unhappy about that, but we are pleased that part of the agreement is that the times when votes will be taken will not come as a surprise to anyone. The votes on the two report stage amendments will come at the end of the first day on which the debate on Bill C-2 is called again in the fall, and the vote on third reading, the final, crucial vote on this issue, will come at a time to be arranged by agreement among the four House leaders.
I submit that this is an exceedingly fair arrangement. Neither side will win by default on the part of the other side. No one will be caught by surprise. The debate at some point will come to an end, a decision will be made on when a vote is to be taken, so that every member can be here and we can have a clearcut vote on the basis of as full attendance as possible in the House of Commons. So even though some of us may not be completely happy-I suppose that is true for both sides-about the agreement that has been reached, it does seem to me to be a sensible arrangement; and since we have agreed to it on a four party basis, we should be quite prepared to say so and therefore give our support to this motion.
Once this motion is passed, it is likely that there will be some time this afternoon when the House could do some other business, and I press very strongly that the government House leader-or, if he has to leave in the meantime, the acting government House leader-call order No. 12, the order having to do with crop insurance.
We have been trying to negotiate and I know that the negotiations are still going on. Even if we are not able to reach an agreement by negotiations behind the curtains or in the corridors, I think the order should be called. Maybe there are some who want to debate it, so an hour or two could be used for that purpose, but I do not think we should go out of this place today with that order not dealt with because it was not called. It has come back from committee without amendments, I believe. There are not amendments on the report stage, and there is only third reading left. I can speak for my party and say that we are prepared to pass it without debate; but even if there are members of any other party who want to debate it, let us call the order, have the debate and see if we can get that bill through before we leave here this afternoon.
I suggest also that the bill to amend the Aeronautics Act, which has come out of committee and contains certain provisions that the government would like to have enacted, is one that might be dealt with this afternoon as well. I do not use so many words about that because I do not think there is a dispute over that, but surely that could be done as well.
I think also that if there is a statement on feed grains policy-and some of my colleagues may have a few words to say about this later in this debate-has been prepared by the government, then the absence of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) should not stand in the way of that

July 27, 1973

statement being given to the House today. It may well be that the statement has not been prepared. We cannot ask the government for a statement of policy if it has no policy, but if a policy has been brought into being by the government, I think that the time to make that statement is today, even if some other minister has to make it. There will be a great deal of anger if a statement is not made today simply on the excuse that the Minister of Justice is not here, and then he makes it on Monday or Tuesday when the House has gone away. I press that point and, as I said, it may be pressed further by some of my colleagues.
The only other area in which I wish to say a few words has to do with the session that will commence on October 15. Mind you, there could be a session in the meantime if there is an emergency that brings us back. So far as the railway strike situation is concerned, my leader, the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis), has stated very clearly our feeling that for the next week or so it would be better for us not to be here so that the collective bargaining process could go on without the fear that there will be back to work legislation.
With respect to the fall session that will commence on October 15, I want to say without hesitation-despite my interest in other matters of legislation to which I will refer-that we must get the capital punishment issue out of the way first. I know that when it is called there will be some catcalls on the floor of the House as to why we are dealing with capital punishment, why not something else.
However, the capital punishment bill is an important matter of public policy and an important element in the law of the land. We have invested a great deal of parliamentary time in it, and I urge that it be got out of the way in the first six or seven days after we come back in the fall. But then let us give top priority to some of the pressing matters that are before us. The family allowances measure, in my view, should have had second reading a month ago. We did not get it, but the bill is on the order paper and it has been printed. We have seen the bill and there is pretty general support for it. I do not think the debate at second reading needs to be long. Let us pass that bill early when we are back in the fall so that there will be no question about its provisions coming into effect on January 1, 1974.
I urge also that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), in the two and a half months we are now giving him to come up with a few things, be ready in the fall with his other bill on the Canada Pension Plan. I say "other bill" because we do have a little one on the order paper having to do with certain religious groups and a few technical points, but I am referring to the other bill which has been promised, the aim of which is to raise the yearly maximum pensionable earnings under the Canada Pension Plan and also to remove the 2 per cent ceiling on the annual escalation of pensions under the Canada Pension Plan.
It was certainly my understanding when the orange paper, the working paper on social security, was brought in earlier this year that it was the hope and the intention of the government that the changes in the Canada Pension Plan would be effective on January 1, 1974.
Summer Recess
Some of the things that the Minister of National Health and Welfare has said lately have cast some doubt on the certainty of that. I think that has to become a matter of certainty, Mr. Speaker, namely, that the escalation of pensions under the Canada Pension Plan when they next occur, namely at the beginning of 1974, will not be limited to 2 per cent but will at least match the full rise in the cost of living. I put this as a matter of very high priority on our legislative program for the fall. I press it vigorously, because, unlike some of the other things I referred to, it is not on the order paper, but it must get there.
One of the reasons we must get the Canada Pension Plan amending bill before us and get it passed is that there are a dozen other pension plans and arrangements where the annual escalation is still limited to 2 per cent, and the government keeps using the excuse-and no one gives it to us more often than the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury)-that these other plans cannot have the rate of their escalation increased until the rate of escalation is increased under the Canada Pension Plan.
I set that out as a program for this fall; that the Canada Pension Plan bill be brought in and passed, and that all other pension plans that come under the jurisdiction or responsibility of the federal government be dealt with this fall so that in 1974 those escalations will be at least the full extent of the cost of living and not limited to 2 per cent.
Mr. Speaker-yes, I will use the term-it is highway robbery to limit the escalation of any pension to 2 per cent at a time when the cost of living is going up 5 per cent, 6 per cent and 7 per cent. Someone says 8 per cent and maybe by January 1 it will be even more, Mr. Speaker. I put this very high on the priority list; something has to be done about it this year.
I also remind the Minister of National Health and Welfare that in the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs earlier this year, when some pressure was put on him to provide escalation more often than annually, such as semi-annually, quarterly or even monthly, he deprecated that as not having much value and said it might be better to have periodic increases in the basic amount of pensions like old age security. I say to him that, with what is happening to the cost of living and the standard of living generally, the government must not go on thinking that $100 is enough as a basic old age pension. This, too, is something that ought to be considered, but certainly this fall let the months between October 15 and Christmas not pass without dealing with this whole problem. I am speaking of the problem of the annual escalation of pensions under the Canada Pension Plan, pensions for retired civil servants, retired RCMP personnel, retired armed forces personnel, railway pensioners, and all those who are affected by government legislation. Let us have them dealt with this fall without fail.
While these things are dealt with may I remind the House, in case some pension gets missed, that the government passed regulations under the responsibility of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Stanbury) which provide that even private pension plans cannot get income tax consideration unless they hold their escalation to 2 per cent. This is something that is a disgrace. It is highway robbery of our retired people and it can and must be dealt with this fall.

July 27, 1973
Summer Recess
I just want to mention two or three other things that, in my view, should have very high priority this fall. One is the election expenses bill which got to committee. We had hoped that the committee would have dealt with it by now but that has not been the case. That committee should certainly meet in the fall, if not between now and then, and get that bill back so we can get it through before the end of the year. Then there is the bill regarding foreign investment which has been reported out of committee and has been improved considerably. It should be high on the priority list for the fall.
So, Mr. Speaker, I join with those with whom I have contended this week in an attempt to arrive at an agreement by saying that none of us is fully satisfied with the arrangements we have made for the disposal of the capital punishment bill in the fall, but we feel we have reached a sensible agreement. I believe, therefore, that we should welcome and give our support to this motion, but that we should put the government on notice that, not only do we want certain items brought forward this afternoon, but there are these priorities I have dealt with on which we want action as soon as possible after the House returns on October 15.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prince Albert):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is now three minutes to one o'clock and while I do not intend to cover the whole gamut the way the last member did in making again the speech he has made on several occasions, there are a number of things I want to deal with.
It has been an interesting session so far. The government has swallowed itself several times. The west has been discovered by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). The Queen has suddenly ceased to be anathema to the Prime Minister. Chameleons are noted for changing themselves according to their environment. Perhaps during the noon hour some hon. members would like to confirm that in front of the Prime Minister's office there are three sculptures of animals. As well, quite a large expenditure was made for carpets in the hall there. But there is only one animal that should have been placed there as a trademark of this government, and that is the chameleon.
I intend to deal with one or two of these matters, Mr. Speaker. It has been a session in which the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) has started to read American history, and has quoted John Paul Jones. We have just begun to touch on it.
In the last six weeks or so the government apparently has repeatedly changed its mind. Up to that time it could rely at all times, and even now, on the support of the NDP. Mind you, I was disturbed to read the frightening words of the leader of the NDP in Vancouver-I will quote his words later-when he pointed out that the government must now realize that it is in jeopardy. He said that the parliamentary caucus of the NDP cannot tolerate much longer the Trudeau government, but he could not say how long that would be. This represents a complete somersault in attitude.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It being one o'clock I do now leave the chair.
At one o'clock the House took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 2 p.m.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prince Albert):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the numbers present on the government side, which include one minister, one hopeful parliamentary secretary and five members, indicate the interest of the government in public affairs.
Before the House rose for lunch, I had been alluding to the interesting fact that in front of the Prime Minister's office there are costly sofas where the wayfarer may rest and that there are three statues of animals. Having regard to the change of front on the part of this government, I suggest one statue has been omitted, that of the chameleon, which changes colour whenever circumstances or the environment make that necessary in the interest of its survival.
In looking at the remnants of this government, I see the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Sharp) present, and see in his eye that pugnacity which is synonymous with the declaration made the other day that, We have just begun to fight. That was one of the proudest statements anyone ever made. History knows that event turned out all right for the original author. However, when I think of the way in which Canada, in the last few months, has lost standing and status all over the world, I would think that the minister, as head of the Department of External Affairs, would stand up once and for all for Canadian rights all over the world.
I am thinking of one thing in particular, and I will not intrude on the work done in this connection by the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Cossitt). I am thinking of that Canadian who has been in prison in Cuba for over ten years.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: For doing what?
Will the minister tell me?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The right hon. member must know.
Oh, the minister does not know.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: You tell the House.
There was no justification whatsoever for imprisoning that man-

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Not for smuggling arms?
There was no justification-

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Not for smuggling arms?
I will begin to fight in a moment. There was no justification whatever for this government, for the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), not to get in touch with Premier Castro and-

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The right hon. member would not have done it when he was prime minister.

Mr. Speaker, one may make remarks from a seated position that may get on Hansard, but that
July 27, 1973

action does not really show the kind of statesmanship we expect from a man occupying the minister's portfolio.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Nor from a former prime minister.

Mr. Speaker, what manner of mumbling is this that is going on? Sir, even in the days of the aboriginals, if one was speaking and the others had nothing to say, they did not mumble and grumble. All I wish to say is this: the failure of this government to make representations to Castro for the release of Ronald Lippert is disgraceful. After ten years of imprisonment there should be representations on personal and public grounds, having regard to the serious condition of his mother. Of course, I do not expect any action from this government because it will not speak out internationally. Muted words are the only response. All the minister would have to do, with the acquaintanceship between the Prime Minister and Mr. Castro, would be to get in touch with Castro and ask for consideration of this case.
-
We have the same situation in connection with the Canadians who were killed in Africa. We have had nothing but generalities from the minister. Two Canadians were murdered in cold blood. At the same time, the nation which participated in that murder is receiving tremendous grants from our country and will receive further grants. What was the unctuous reply of the minister? He said, you would not expect us to not act to help the poor people of that country by giving assistance? I cannot understand the attitude of this government in the face of what has been done to Canadians. What is the reward? The reward is hundreds of thousands of dollars of extra money to that country which has not done anything to expiate the crime committed in the murder of two Canadians. I hope the minister will, with regard to international actions, have his own department adopt those strident words, we have just begun to fight.
I was going to refer at some length to the New Democratic Party. In the absence of the leader of that party, I am not going to do that. I never do. I quoted his statement this morning, so the quotation will be clear. The leader of the New Democratic Party, speaking in Vancouver, said:
"I can't tell you when the next election will take place but I find it difficult to imagine being able to tolerate the Trudeau government much longer."
Hear, hear!

The NDP are now all together. Until that statement, they were divided. Is there any wonder there is an article in today's Ottawa Citizen headed "NDP looking for divorce from Grits". They are right up to date and have already joined in the applause. James Ferrabee, a very experienced and responsible writer, says and I quote:
The marriage of convenience is over. It's now only a question of finding a good pretext for divorce.
Are they applauding again?

Hear, hear!
Summer Recess

They are. That is what they are waiting for. Once you get the approval of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), you know where the party is going and he approved that statement. I say to the government, watch out; be careful, because the hon. member has applauded that suggestion. They are just waiting for an excuse. I do not know what the grounds for divorce are politically. No doubt it is the indecency of dilly-dally by the government that is going to form the basis for this unusual occurrence.
What are some of the other matters with which we have not dealt? I would like the Acting Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) to give us some idea of what happened on the safari to Calgary. There was a tremendous build-up. The Prime Minister found that western Canada existed. He admitted it. How could people live in three provinces and the Prime Minister not know they existed? That was difficult in itself, but it was even more difficult when he had to go to the provincial premiers to find out what western Canada needed.
Did the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson), that well-known agriculturalist, not speak to the government about that? What about God's gift to the Liberal party from Saskatchewan, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang)? Did he not let them in on the secret? What about Mahoney who has risen to great heights since the election in return for value received? What about the former Minister of Agriculture, Mr. Olson? Did he not let the government know?
Then, we come to British Columbia. There are two ministers from that province. They are not here now. Have they not let the government in on the secret? Do they hold cabinet meetings in secret in which ministers cannot speak? I get an affirmative answer by a bow of the head of the Acting Prime Minister.
They have just begun to fight.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) says they have just begun to fight.
Hear, hear!

This is a most preposterous situation. Did the Minister of Justice not let the government know what the result would be with this tinkering in connection with the so-called two price system? Did he not let them know the farmers in western Canada will get less this year than last?
That is not true.

I suggest that again the Acting Prime Minister moves his head indicating a negative reply. If he would just stay in international affairs, he would learn just as much about them as he apparently has about agriculture. I remind him of this.
