The other day I said the price of bread would increase from one to four cents a loaf as a result of this tinkering. The Prime Minister said there was no foundation for that. He said it would only be about one-tenth of one per cent.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Quote him correctly. Quote from Hansard, not newspapers.

July 27, 1973
Summer Recess
What is that babble?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Be fair.

I am glad the minister, knowing nothing about the situation, wants some information. If he wants to speak, I will give him an opportunity, but if he does not have any written material before him I know he will not say anything. I quote from an article in the Vancouver Sun, home edition, of July 24:
Bread price to go up two or three cents
A flour milling firm spokesman today said the price of bread will go up two or three cents a loaf as a result of new wheat prices.
He went on to say that the price of flour had been raised by a very considerable amount to $6.50 per hundredweight, an increase of 45 cents to 55 cents a bushel charged millers by the wheat board. The Prime Minister said there was nothing to it. He had not been to the provincial premiers' meeting at that time. He had not discovered the west. He had not followed in the footsteps of Henry Kelsey who was there in 1691.
yesterday, flour increased by $2.35 per hundredweight. What is the government doing about it? Nothing. It refuses to face the situation. When I raised this matter in the House last week, the Prime Minister brushed it aside. He said there was nothing to it. The government refuses to act. The cost of living of the average Canadian will go up very considerably as a result of this increase in the price of bread. What does the government say it will do? First, it says there will be no increase. When it does happen, I suppose they will turn it over to this board with the $40,000 a year chairman for the purpose of ascertaining whether anything took place. Why does the government not act?
I should like to deal next with the remarks of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro). He was here this morning. He spoke and he left. What a picture! He gave us a lecture on conciliation procedures and labour discussions. Nobody is in disagreement with that. But when it comes to acting and doing, there is nothing to report. I do not blame him, because he does not know anything about the subject; he gets his direction from someone else.
I asked him what he intended to do about the dispute between the company and the non-operating railway employees, as reported at page 5988 of Hansard. He said he did not believe there was any immediate danger. I was dealing with the shipment of wheat. Then, I asked this question:
How long does the government anticipate this state of affairs will continue before parliament will act so that the economy of the nation will not be unnecessarily weakened? Has the government any plans in this regard or does it simply intend to paddle along day by day?
The word "paddle" was well chosen judging from the general attitude of the minister this morning. In reply, he said that historically, as he understood it, the Conservative party had always stood for free collective bargaining and for giving people their legitimate rights as recognized by parliament. He went on to say:
I think the parties should be allowed to bargain in a free and collective way. When the public interest is at stake I think the
government will exercise its responsibility, but I hope that will not be necessary.
I ask him today: When is he going to act? What has he been doing in the last few weeks? From the explanation he gave today, it is obvious the answer is that he has just been sitting on the problem. He refuses to face it. He has refused to accept any of the suggestions made to the government. He is just waiting around, and while he waits the economic situation becomes worse. Immediately upon conclusion of his statement this morning, I asked him a question. I asked him: When are you going to act? And what did we get by way of reply? A massive explanation with many words but a total failure to convey any idea of when the government proposes to act.
As to the motion we are considering, I say at once that when agreements have been entered into among the representatives of the parties, they must be upheld. But what is behind all this? Is this sudden desire for an adjournment the result of the fact that the government does not intend to do anything regarding the cost of living? Is another reason the fact that it does not want parliament to be sitting while the price of bread goes up, not as a result of the forces of demand and supply but as a result of a government action which cannot be justified?
Hear, hear!

There can be no question that this is the situation. They are afraid to have the House in session. They do not want to have this subject discussed.
Again, there is the question of feed grain, dealt with by one of the hon. members who preceded me. Why does the government not make a declaration? The Minister of Justice almost torpedoed the western meeting with the provincial premiers by his lack of finesse in saying he was afraid those various premiers were using tunnel vision. Why has the hon. member no revelation to make as to whether feed grains are to be taken from the Wheat Board? Certainly, if this were done when parliament were sitting, the government would know where it stood. We have made that perfectly clear. I warn the Acting Prime Minister that if the announcement is made after parliament has adjourned that feed grains are to be taken from the Wheat Board there will be an explosion on the Prairies which will make the nuclear explosion at Nagasaki look like a fire cracker parade on May 24.
Why is there no announcement? Has a decision been made? For weeks the Minister of Justice has been going about intimating that some great announcement would be made, but that it would not be made until after the conference of the premiers. Well, the conference is over. The Minister of Justice is not here. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) is not here. Why has there been no announcement? In the last election the Liberal party ended up with no seats in Alberta. It did a little better in Saskatchewan, and a little better in Manitoba. Let me say this to hon. members on the other side of the House, and let me make it abundantly clear: if you start this nonsense in connection with feed grains you will not have enough Liberal elected members in the next election to provide seed for the one after!

Oh, oh!

July 27, 1973

I do not know what the Minister of Labour really has in mind. I do not know whether he has any plan in mind. I was very interested to hear that in the month of June the Liberal Party went into solemn conclave to decide whether or not they might go into a kind of retreat called transcendental meditation. Is that what they want to do during the next couple of months?
There is even division over there. There is the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Cafik). I like him. He comes from a constituency and an area where I was raised as a boy. I like him, and I have never heard him more outspoken that he was today. I have always said, and I have been criticized for it, that parliamentary secretaries should not be answering questions in this House because they have no responsibility. I have said I would not be answered by a parliamentary secretary because they are helpmates of the ministers and have none of the responsibilities of cabinet knowledge or authority. I say to him: Beware! After a speech like that today there is likely to be a vacancy during the period when parliament is not sitting. I am amazed at the strength of the attack the hon. member made on the Department of Transport. It was harsh. It showed the department acting in a way which, to say the least, was inexcusable. The hon. member bows his head in full approval. They have been at it for two years. No, for three years- beg your pardon, Mr. Speaker, I am always conservative.
Hear, hear!

Even the mountain, when it laboured, brought forth a mouse. For three years, he, with knowledge none of the rest of us can possess, by reason of his propinquity to the powers that be, has been unable to discern what the government may do. That speech deserves the utmost consideration by every member of the House for it represents only the second occasion on which, since the present government was elected last fall, any member supporting that administration has dared to speak against it.
They don't think Trudeau tells the truth.

Western farmers have not forgotten that Mr. Trudeau did not know they raise wheat. He had no idea about that. He had been all over the world, to China, the U.S.S.R. and elsewhere but he did not know that. He said in Winnipeg he did not know the Wheat Board existed, yet he is the Prime Minister. He asked: "Do you expect me to sell wheat?" The farmers have not forgotten that.
What is the government doing today? I see the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) is here.
Hear, hear!

The Minister of Finance has promised to "debank" the banks. I want to say to him that out of that conference, and the announcement could have been made in the House without consultation with the provincial premiers, has come that declaration. I join in giving it my approval as it is the one thing that came out of the
Summer Recess
conference, or rather out of the mouths of the ministers at the conference, which enabled them to place before the western premiers something that had been done.
I ask what is going to be done to help the farmers, to give them an additional amount at this time? The plan that he has evolved which masquerades now as a two-price system, is simply a complete delusion and a sham. What this government did was ascertain how much wheat would be consumed in Canada, and then it fixed a fair price for that wheat. That fair price brought about a quotient and that quotient was to be divided as evidence of a two-price system. I have already pointed out what is going to happen to the price of bread as a result of that action. This government would not introduce a system of acreage payments. Oh, no, it would not do that because a Conservative government had done it. We are going to have a two-price system so that wheat farmers will get a fair return, but they are making payments under it in respect of all grains, wheat, oats, barley and every other variety, and it will not cost the government anything.
I find the Minister of Finance is one who listens. I suggest to him that the very first thing that should be done now, and it will prevent the rise in the price of flour and bread, is simply to take the $60 million, which is the amount that we distributed by way of acreage payments and is the amount this government is bonusing the baking industry, and pay it out on an acreage basis. You will get the farm support for that action. It is a course we followed. At the same time, you will stop another increase in the cost of living across this country, namely the increase in the cost of bread which will affect every home in this nation.
The government will not do that. The government has not even listened to the variety of individuals who surround the throne. When I was Prime Minister it cost $50,000 to run the Prime Minister's office. Today, it costs $1,300,000, and it only cost $25,000 more under Mr. Pearson than it cost when I was Prime Minister. There are hoards of individuals.
Shadows.
Shadows at least have some existence. All these people are doing is drawing tremendous salaries.
Hear, hear!

They have desks for the east, the west, the north and the south to tell them what the western provinces and other provinces desire. It has cost us hundreds of thousands of dollars for these desks, yet the government did not have any information regarding the western provinces. What do these people do? Are they decorations? What responsibility do they have? They simply gather together and pretend they are doing something. I suggest that none of the views of these people are passed on to the government. If any minister will say to me that they are, my simple question would then be, show me one example that the government has followed. There is not one single example of any change that has taken place to the benefit of the western provinces, Alberta, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and B.C., as the result of this western desk.

July 27, 1973
Summer Recess
I notice there has been no endeavour to explain why there has been so little for the western provinces out of the fabulous expenditures under DREE across this country. Why is it that we in the province of Saskatchewan received a paltry $1.5 million out of these vast expenditures? Now, in 1973, after the shellacking this government took in the election it has suddenly realized that the west exists. Mr. Marchand has said: "Well, now I can see the picture". Those were his views, and they are going to do a lot more for western Canada. All I have to say is go ahead and do it, but if you think the people of western Canada will believe there is any sincerity in what you are doing I can only tell you that the conclusion they will come to, and it is a proper one, is that you are endeavouring to get forgiveness for the wrongs you have done in forgetting the west throughout the last several years.
There are other matters I could deal with but I am not going to on this occasion, except to say this: It was a great meeting in Calgary.
A dandy.

The minister gives it approval. When it came to sartorical perfection and masculine attractiveness on television I have to give it marks, and I am not going to start to identify. One has to give it marks, but what did it accomplish? Why did the ministers not take the advice of the opposition members representing those western provinces who over and over again placed these matters before them? Do not let the government, even the Acting Prime Minister, believe that it has deluded anybody in western Canada by this massive endeavour of propaganda and deception, and that is all it was.
When the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) advanced any of these matters he was ridiculed. When members of the opposition advanced these matters they were ridiculed. When members of the NDP placed views before the House that could be generally accepted, they were ridiculed. Then, suddenly the Prime Minister had to admit they were right. You talk about the road to Damascus, but I remind you that this Prime Minister said he never realized the west existed. We have lived out there many years and we are certainly glad that the Prime Minister knows we exist.
I warn the government that on the basis of its failure to act on behalf of western farmers, and on behalf of expansion of industrial opportunity, not only in the west but also in the Maritimes, when the election comes they will get their reward and it will not be what they expect, or possibly they do. They cannot get away with such deception.
I conclude by saying that the animal which is able to change its colour and appearance whatever the environment now has a counterpart in the Prime Minister, but this will not work.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I did not know whether I was listening to the opening speech in an election campaign, and it may be that the right hon. gentleman, like many of us, was speaking for his constituency, because as I gather from the machinations that

have taken place recently we are not headed into an election but are facing another session this fall.
The right hon. gentleman outlined many of the problems we have, but I think it would have been better had he considered the problem we have been faced with during the last month. I refer to the problem of a regular recess, not necessarily one set by agreement, for the months of July and August. We have heard from two House leaders this afternoon. Probably it could be detected in the remarks of the third House leader who spoke that the agreement on the motion before us was reached not because of their efforts but because the government more or less forced it on them. This raises in my mind a problem I have mentioned on many other occasions; that is, the desirability, if this parliament is to sit for 10 months, that we at least have the common sense to arrange our sittings so that in this northern hemisphere, where our summer if we are lucky lasts for the months of July and August, these be the two months in which we have our summer recess. There is absolutely no reason for sitting here in the month of July.
There would have been a reason had the government decided it would do something about capital punishment. But what happened in respect of capital punishment? The greatest offender in respect of having some decision, good or bad, reached with regard to capital punishment was the Solicitor General. There have been at least three bad Solicitors General and they keep getting worse. The previous Solicitor General had absolutely no understanding of the fact that most of this country operates under the common law. He believed everybody operated under the Napoleonic Code. So, he really did not understand the law relating to the British system. This is the reason there were so many mistakes made in respect of the penitentiary system, the parole system and other matters.
The present Solicitor General, however, does know something about these things. He introduced the debate on capital punishment, but he kept putting not only one foot in his mouth but both feet. This is not a very benevolent place and, therefore, I am surprised how benevolent it has been in respect of the present Solicitor General as he keeps changing feet. Everyone seems to feel sorry for him. Had this debate been conducted by the House leaders rather than by the Solicitor General, it would have been a simple matter of deciding whether or not we would have capital punishment for an additional five years in the same manner as we had the original five year period.
The Solicitor General, however, adds all sorts of things. He allowed the introduction of the female chauvinist resolution. He allowed the introduction of a number of other additional items, most of them at his own insistence. Then, he decided after making these arrangements that he would go for total abolition. How could there be anything so stupid? He could not have listened to the vast majority of the speeches in the House on the three previous occasions when this matter was before the House.
The House leaders are partly responsible for the mess in which we find ourselves. Certainly, the government House leader was responsible for it because when he keeps changing priorities in respect of items which he believes
July 27, 1973

are absolutely necessary he cannot count on the co-operation of the other House leaders and cannot count on the co-operation of the members. Sooner or later, we should make the decision that we will be here for regular four-year periods barring other developments because of the democratic process. This being the case we should count on having regular holidays.
You may remember, Mr. Speaker, the one time we had no Easter recess simply because, when the House could not make up its mind, I insisted that we sit on Good Friday. We sat on that occasion just long enough to adjourn, and since that time there has been no problem in respect of having an Easter recess. It is now a formal arrangement. As intelligent adults, we obviously ought to be able to arrive, in this northern hemisphere, at a point where we decide that our vacation period will be held in the summer, a time when members will be able to visit the farmers working in the fields and visit the people at their leisure. If I were in the southern hemisphere I would perhaps be recommending that we have our holiday in the winter. The government House leader should visit northern Ontario. This is the first summer in three years in which we have had summer weather. This chamber is not the place in which members should be enjoying summer. In my opinion when this happens very little is accomplished in this place.
I am concerned about the remarks made today in relation to settling labour disputes. Sooner or later, I believe we must decide that the federal government should not be muddling around in negotiations. In this present situation I understand that the negotiations concern pensions on Canadian National Railways. There is a great deal of interest in pensions. The average worker on the railway does not trust his union leaders. In the field of pensions, there probably will not be any settlement even if this parliament decides there will be. We have reached the stage where members call on the government to bring in legislation just as a strike begins, even though it is merely a rotating strike which affects a very limited number of communities in this country.
I would like to see legislation passed in respect of Canadian Pacific Airlines. It seems to me this would be a good time to bring it under Air Canada so that we can make up our minds which airline is to fly to Rome and which airline is to provide domestic services. In my area Air Canada has suddenly decided that it does not have aircraft suitable for service in northern Quebec or northern Ontario. It is ready to give the service to somebody else and if no one wants it; then Air Canada will desert the field. This problem relates to the line between the area of the one member for Timiskaming and the other member for Temiscamingue. Air Canada seems to have shut off any sort of service on a regional basis between northern Ontario and northern Quebec.
It may interest hon. members to know that there may be other reasons for this situation. Recently, an organization has been established in North Bay which is interested in vigorously pursuing the establishment of a new province in northern Ontario. There has always been a reciprocal movement in northwestern Quebec which believes it could well join with northeastern Ontario in setting up a new province based mainly on resources.
Summer Recess
Oh, no.

The Minister of Finance says no. Certainly this is no more possible than that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) should follow Social Credit philosophy and double the value of Canadian currency. I admit that this is a field about which I do not know too much, but it is supposed to be something about which the minister knows, so at least let him give me credit for knowing that the people are dissatisfied.
I do not know how the people in his department will feel about the kooky arrangement in which we find ourselves. We may be back here in two weeks. I am intrigued by the argument that is being put forward that we had better leave before somebody forces us into legislating against the strike, and that is why we need the recess. We have all agreed to go home from today until October 15. I do not know how many families will be home to see their MP when he is in the constituency between the end of July and October 15. In my area even the fall fairs will be over. I will be able to go to the ploughing matches, but they only last so long. Mr. Speaker, by then it will be snowing and the weather will not be sufficiently good to allow us to go anywhere.
This year there will not be an election because I believe all the politcal parties have made that decision. Certainly the Liberals will not call one. They are sending the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to Peking when the fall session of parliament opens, and Mao Tse-tung will not give him any advice that will influence him much, even with regard to the province of Quebec. I do not think the Prime Minister will be able to change the situation there, nor will he be able to change it in the west. So I do not expect that during his trip to China an election will be called here. I do not see any way in which any members of the House can cause an election to be called. There will probably be more goodies in the throne speech, which will be supported, and more goodies in the budget, which will also be supported.
Frankly, I have begun to look forward to the budget now that we are in the business of printing money without any backing. I would like the minister, whom I have always found to be fairly responsible, to have a long, serious talk with two of his colleagues, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) and the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson), for the purpose of getting the gold mines operating again. We now have a fairly good price for gold and at least the minister will be able to back some of the money with gold, particularly if he puts it in the treasury at $38 an ounce and sells it on the European bullion market at $125. I can think of no better way in which to correct the mistakes he has made in the last few days than to embark upon the production of gold immediately and sell it on the European market.
This raises another problem that I have, that is, that we should be providing assistance to the gold mines. This would be very useful to northern Ontario and many other areas where the rate of unemployment is high. This is the type of industry that we have supported on many occasions simply because our monetary system depended upon

July 27, 1973
Summer Recess
it. I suggest that that situation has not really changed, although certainly our ideas have changed. The production of gold in this country may provide a valuable bulwark against the decline of the American dollar. When that decline results in the fall of an empire, Canada will not, unless it has a separate basis for protecting its existence, find itself in too happy a situation.
There are many matters that could be raised. My colleagues have been very concerned about the crop insurance legislation not having been debated. They will probably have something to say about that. I know that the feed grains legislation has concerned some of my colleagues. One of my colleagues has expressed concern about the proposed sale, which the government is allowing, of the Bessborough Hotel in Saskatoon. I do not know whether the Minister of Finance has ever stayed at the Bessborough. I have found it to be a fairly good hotel. Yet I am informed it is up for sale, that it will be no more a property of the CNR but will go into the hands of a new group. Also, my colleagues are concerned that the Minister of Finance has not been here to answer a number of questions regarding his delay in the appointment of CNR auditors. I agree that he had very legitimate reasons for firing Mr. Benson's auditors for the CNR, but why has he not appointed new ones?
Let the bill go to committee.

I think we have an agreement that we will allow the government to appoint them, and certainly I do not think the bill is needed for that. But if the minister wants to scribble out a small bill now, we would be prepared to pass it this afternoon and have the auditors appointed. Let him not hide behind that excuse. The Auditor General is being paid to do that audit. He can sit down with his staff and prepare it, and we can look at the matter of CNR financing.
The Minister of Finance knows that he has been allowing the CNR to borrow money rather than let us provide the money, as is done in normal financing practice. We have not considered CNR financing for the last two years, and this will catch up with the CNR in terms of the interest which will be compounded on top of the other interest which we have to pay now. The minister shakes his head. Obviously, he knows that there is a greater expenditure on the interest rate for the financing of CNR than there is profit. He is well aware of that fact. The profit is usually about $28 million, and our expenditure on interest amounts to around $70 million. To compound that interest by allowing CNR to borrow money rather than having the government finance the railway seems to be a waste of time.
My reason for rising is to make a plea to the House. My request will not be granted now, in all probability, and I am not suggesting that we consider it now. I make a plea that as adults, as people many of whom have had some experience in business where there is some order, we demand of our caucuses and our House leaders that an agreement be reached to allow for an orderly system of recessing parliament for the summer. This business of everybody negotiating at the end of June for new priorities and new emergencies for which legislation must be

passed is a ridiculous way of operating. For three years we have tried to set July, August and September aside for a summer recess. My guess is that by sitting until July we assure ourselves of having to sit until the end of July next year.
The fact that we have put off the date of our return for the regular session until the middle of October almost guarantees that the work of the House cannot be completed in a reasonable period of time so as to assure us of a recess at the end of next June.
I know that this presents problems to the government House leader, for whom I have great respect-and I have had dealings with a number of House leaders. I find the government House leader to be honest and generous. In fact, often he is too generous with the people with whom he associates. He makes all sorts of concessions which in my opinion it would be better not to make. I suggest, also, that he should be treated fairly by other members of the House, and in particular by the cabinet. It seems to me unreasonable that the cabinet should continually hold over his head the threat of putting forward another piece of emergency legislation at the last minute. By the end of May he should be able to tell the House exactly what he wants passed before the end of June, and we should have the discipline to keep that schedule.
If you look back, you will find that if the type of agreement that has been worked out had been made at the end of May, then there would have been other pieces of legislation that would have been deemed just as urgent as Bill C-2. I believe that members of parliament each have a responsibility. It is all right to go to your caucus and say "me too" all the time, but it seems to me you should have some guts and be prepared to take a position in caucus that would bring about some order. Most hon. members were not here when the fight took place over a period of eight or ten years for an orderly Christmas and an orderly Easter recess. The solution was not arrived at too easily.
I suggest that every member has a responsibility to see that we do not again get into the box we are in today because of our inability to set a predetermined recess period which, in the northern part of the North American continent, should be the months when the children are out of school, July and August. This is not going to be done by the government nor by the opposition; it is going to be done by the backbenchers who have not the pressure that I am sure individual cabinet ministers have to get their particular pieces of legislation through. The ministers say to themselves that if they wait another two or three hot days they will get their bill through. It may be necessary for some of us to become obnoxious and to take the position that we are going to force the government to arrive at that kind of conclusion. I am sure there are many who agree with me that the recess should not be arranged as it has been now, with the threat of a deadline and the threat of other action, during this last two month period. We should have a more orderly method of arranging it.
Mr. Speaker, I have made this speech before. I am surprised that it has not lent itself to the consideration of the government. When the late Mr. Pearson was leader of the government, for some reason or other, he supported
July 27, 1973

the suggestion and for three or four years we did have a recess during July and August. Perhaps the decision was made even before that.

Let us in on the
conversation.

Again, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) has something to say. Mr. Speaker, during the time that he was Minister of Justice he never had a piece of legislation passed that he designed himself; it was all there from the previous minister of justice. The same is true of the present minister of justice; his legislation came from the previous minister. Nothing moves very fast in this place, Mr. Speaker. That is why I am making my pitch now, so that members will have an opportunity to give it full consideration before next year. We have spoiled most of this year, but I am hopeful that members will seriously consider doing something about the recess next year. I shall certainly start a little earlier to do my part to see that my objective is achieved.

Mr. Speaker, I do not want to take too long to say what I have to say but I think it should be said this afternoon. I want to remind the House that we are about to adjourn today having left hanging a matter of considerable importance, especially to the west coast of British Columbia. I refer, of course, to the recent events that have taken place with respect to the United States legislation approving the TAPS oil tanker route and the confusion regarding the Canadian position up until now. I want to remind hon. members that we have been faced with these problems since 1968, and throughout this entire period of time the government has, in one way or another, attempted to assure the people on the west coast that everything possible was being done, not just to keep tankers out of Puget Sound as has been suggested recently, but to stop the tanker route.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, that is not so. The hon. member knows that is not so.

The hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) interrupts and says that is not so. That has not been the thrust of the remarks of members speaking on behalf of the Liberal Party in Vancouver over the past several years. There is no question that the present Leader of the Liberal Party in British Columbia

July 27, 1973
Summer Recess
has been adamantly opposed to a tanker route, and throughout the last election campaign he had support on this point from members of the Liberal Party, both new candidates and those standing for re-election.
No matter what the minister may want to say now, I say that the position of the government today is not the position that people on the west coast thought they were taking earlier. The position of the government today is that our only concern has always been to keep tankers out of Puget Sound. If that is so, why has there been no attempt to offer an oil pipeline to the Americans if they would apply to the National Energy Board, as an alternative? After all, an oil pipeline had to be an alternative to the tanker route, not just to the tankers in Puget Sound.
The fact of the matter is, Mr. Speaker, that in 1971 the former minister for energy, mines and resources met with the companies involved in the Prudhoe oil fields and they made it quite clear that they would not fight the National Energy Board for a trans-Canadian oil pipeline. At that point, unless the Canadian government was prepared to adjust its position and enter into some sort of agreement, treaty or otherwise, with the Americans, it was clear that no matter how long we kept saying we invited an application to the National Energy Board, no invitation was going to come.
It seems incredible to me that we now say "what a shame the Americans did not accept our invitation" when we have known since 1971 that they would not. I see that the Secretary of State for External Affairs is agitated about some of my remarks. He says that perhaps my interpretation-I put that the kindest way I can-is not correct as to the government's position. If that is so, Mr. Speaker, how is it that on March 2, 1973 in answer to a question I asked in the House, the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was lauding the former member for Esquimalt-Saanich now the Liberal leader in British Columbia, David Anderson? He lauded Mr. Anderson and the quoted words are "for the very good turn of events". We have now reached the incredible position where the Americans finally have to come to us with a specific set of questions which we answered on June 27, which we changed on July 6, which we then told them about by telephone and which we delivered on July 16. My colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs would agree that that has to be the definitive point in terms of diplomacy. We made our delivery and the Prime Minister's remarks were reported in the press, but that was one day before the Unites States Senate voted on it.
Mr. Speaker, I cannot go back and change what has happened. However, I should like to remind all hon. members that we have not appeared credible on this particular issue in terms of our diplomatic action. Second, the government does not look credible to people who have been concerned about this. What happened? On July 18 the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) moved a motion to send a parliamentary delegation to the United States. It did not have the leadership of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the government to clarify the situation with our United States friends. The following day, the New Democratic Party moved a motion to send a parliamentary delegation from the Interparliamentary Union. This did not have the leadership of the government. Apparently it
did not even have the aegis of the government. On July 25, as recorded at page 5965 of Hansard, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) said:
They went without instructions from the government and they will not report to us.
This committee did go to Washington. As the Secretary of State for External Affairs fairly and properly said the other day, some good may well have come of this. I thank him for saying that. He also indicated he perhaps would have a report, but there has been no report. There has been no arrangement whereby members of this committee can meet with ministers of the Crown to discuss what took place the other day in Washington. Nor has any arrangement been made for a debate on this matter.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs now says that the Americans have definitely decided to go ahead with the TAPS line, and that, to use his great words, we have just begun to fight. What in the name of heaven is the use of starting to fight after the battle is over?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The battle is not over. It has not begun.
The minister says the battle is not over. I'll say it is not over, but most of it is being waged on the opposition side of this House to try and get the government to do something.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Why are you so defeatist about it?

We are going to adjourn for two and a half months. We will perhaps be back here in October. We are leaving without any assurance from the government as to what this government is going to do about meeting with this committee who went to see our American counterparts. We do not know the position of the government as to whether we have a quid pro quo from our American friends to supply Canadian oil. We are not having a debate on this subject of vital importance. We are faced with a long adjournment. We will not be back until the middle of the autumn. As far as we are concerned, if what has happened in the past is any indication, nothing more will happen.
I ask hon. members on the government side to consider this. We cannot change what has happened, but there is a great moral responsibility on the government to act. I think the Secretary of State for External Affairs wants to act. I invite him immediately to call together some of the members of the committee and arrange to meet within the next week so that some co-ordinate action can be taken by this country to keep the tankers out of the Pugit Sound area. The government owes that much to the House and to hon. members who have been involved in this question. It owes that much to the Liberal member from British Columbia whom I will be the first to applaud for his heroic and apparently very lonely fight in opposing this tanker route.
I beg the government not to let this matter slide. Otherwise we will adjourn without a meeting of this committee, without government negotiations with the United States, without a debate and without a position. If this process

July 27, 1973

continues, we will be adjourning without a hope of stopping tankers in Pugit Sound.

Mr. Speaker, I will be to the point. Earlier in the debate the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), the hon.

member for York South (Mr. Lewis) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) referred to the fact the minister in charge of the wheat board made a commitment to announce his new feed grains policy before the House adjourned for the summer recess. I think it is regrettable that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) in charge of the Wheat Board is not here today to make a statement about the new feed grains policy. In these circumstances, the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Sharp) or some other minister should rise on motions to tell us what the new policy is to be.
The farmers on the prairies are most concerned. The farmers unions, the co-operatives, the wheat pools, are most anxious that the government not remove feed grain from the jurisdiction of the Wheat Board. It is important that the authority of the board to market feed grain should not be eroded. The right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) was absolutely correct in saying that, if the government were to do this, the uproar on the prairies would be greater than ever before, that the Liberal party there would be totally annihilated because, to the people of the west, the Wheat Board is in many ways what collective bargaining is to a union man-something fundamental.
The orderly marketing of grain is important if a decent price to the farmers is to be maintained. It is also important to the consumers if they do not wish to see the price of food escalating year after year. I have it on good authority from people in the department concerned that a policy was decided on as long ago as March or April of this year. If this is the case, I strongly urge the Acting Prime Minister to make a statement on motions today telling the farmers and the people generally what they may expect in the future.
I am sure the Minister of Justice has deliberately chosen not to appear today because he does not wish to make a statement in the House. He does not want members of opposition parties to be given the opportunity to reply in this chamber where a reply ought to be made. The crop year ends on Tuesday of this week, at the end of July, and the minister must make his announcement by then.
I suggest he is deliberately withholding it in order to make such an announcement outside the House on Monday or Tuesday. I do not think any of the opposition parties want this to happen. The minister should not weaken the powers of the Board. On the contrary, he ought to increase the authority of the Board, giving it jurisdiction over more grains so as to offer farmers a better guarantee of decent prices.
The crop insurance bill has now been considered in committee. No amendments have been made to it. The party to which I belong is prepared to pass this bill without debate. I plead with the government House leader to bring it down so that it may be approved without debate. This would facilitate action by the governments of the prairie provinces which have anticipated that the bill would be passed. It is important that before the House rises the bill should go through, and I believe we could secure an all-party agreement to this effect.

Mr. Speaker, the Progressive Conservative party sent a delegation of western members of parliament to observe the western economic opportunities conference held in Calgary this week. I was one of those delegates and I have come to the House today to state that the national government has once more pulled off a gigantic public relations spectacular, but that their wooing of the west was not reciprocated. Indeed, the Liberals are as jilted today in the west as they were last October 30. And the reason is plain. The one thing the western premiers sought above all else was precisely what they failed to attain, namely, a new attitude by Ottawa toward the west.
Even from a distance, the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) was able to observe the propaganda which dominated and characterized the meetings in Calgary. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) came to the conference with a massive amount of documents which said little except that Ottawa was looking after the west. Various ministers then took turns lecturing the premiers in a condescending manner. The premiers submitted short position papers on four subjects, transportation, industrial development, agriculture and capital financing, in which they made specific proposals. Taken together, these proposals would have formed the basis of a new national policy.
Some of the proposals, such as disclosure of freight rate costs on a limited and confidential basis and the provision enabling provinces to own partial equity in banks, were accepted. But the federal government made only small concessions in areas in which the premiers wanted major action; for example, the amendment of the National Transportation Act to specify that a major objective of the legislatures is the fostering of regional development. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mar-chand) flatly refused that submission. I strongly support the request that this be written into law. Failure to provide such a legislative guarantee means that the west must continue to plead for economic justice rather than receive it by law.
Here we see clearly the way in which Ottawa has again missed the boat. The Prime Minister and his colleagues thought they could soothe western discontent by offering some goodies and promising more subsidies. It is not subsidies or special privileges that the west wants but the removal of federal barriers such as the iniquitous freight rate structure and the injurious tariff system which hinder diversified development in the west. The Calgary conference showed that the Liberal government still fails to understand or appreciate the potential and vitality of the west and its capability to solve its own problems.
It is little wonder that Premier Lougheed of Alberta should have said at the conclusion of the conference; Frankly, we would have forsaken any federal dollars, any federal programs, in exchange for improved understanding. We are not looking for special privileges but to avoid unnecessary obstacles .. . We feel we made some limited progress but we still feel fenced in.
Premier Blakeney of Saskatchewan said at the closure of the conference;
I regret to say that after three days I did not see any progress toward that new national policy.


It was difficult in Calgary to escape the conclusion that the government was more interested in the future of the Liberal party in the west than in the future of the west itself. When it comes to slick salesmanship, nobody can beat the Liberals; but as the western conference clearly showed, they do not have the goods to back up the talk.
Finally, I wish to point out that practically nothing was said at Calgary about western potential and problems which has not been said many times in the House of Commons by western members of parliament. But the government does not listen to members of parliament, especially to western members of parliament. When the government does become serious about the west, its ministers run out to see the premiers, bypassing the representatives who were elected to bring regional concerns before the national forum. I protest the subverting by the government of the legitimate role of members of parliament. We all recall that the Prime Minister used to assert that federal M.P.s from Quebec were the representatives of that province, not the provincial government. In dealing with the west, he bypasses the M.P.s. Could this possibly be because 61 of the 68 western members of parliament are not Liberals?
Since the government wants, to quote the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in Calgary, "a stronger western voice in national decision-making", I urge the government to pay more attention to what western members of parliament advocate in parliament. Televised regional conferences as a showcase for the exhibition of political talent is undoubtedly a powerful weapon for the government, but we are in danger of their becoming substituted for parliament as the central forum for the conducting of national business.
I say to my colleagues from the Atlantic provinces, maybe you would like to have an Atlantic economic opportunities conference, but watch out. If this government sets up such a conference, it will use you for its own political advantages as it has just attempted to use the west. The result will be a lot of local excitement, and when the federal people go back to their enclaves in Ottawa, life will go on the same.

SUGGESTION RECREATIONAL FACILITIES BE FINANCED BY SALE OF COINS AND LOTTERIES-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of national importance to seek leave under Standing Order 43 to move, seconded by the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom):
That this House urge the government to provide communities across Canada with ice rinks, stadia and swimming pools and other urgently needed sports and recreational facilities through a $500 million fund to be financed by the sale of commemorative coins and stamps and a national lottery.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: SUGGESTION RECREATIONAL FACILITIES BE FINANCED BY SALE OF COINS AND LOTTERIES-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
I am sure this motion is submitted with a degree of levity and that the hon. member does not propose that it be put. Unless there is a motion under Standing Order 43 to abolish Standing Order 43, I suggest to the House that we might rise to the call of the bells.
July 27, 1973
